questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: identify the encapsulation break in a reference-returning accessor
questions.stem: A roster class keeps its members in a private String[] names, and its accessor is written as public String[] getNames() { return names; }. What does that accessor hand a client?

options.text: A live handle on the roster's own array, so edits land in the class
A private duplicate that only reads can reach
options.misconception: returning a reference counts as copying

options.text: A defensive copy rebuilt on every single call
options.misconception: every getter must copy by default

options.text: A frozen text summary of the current roster
options.misconception: an array accessor behaves like toString

questions.explanation: Returning the field passes the array reference itself, so the caller and the object share one array and every write through it becomes a write to the roster. The tempting belief is that private hides the contents too, but private hides only the name, and encapsulation is gone the moment a reference to the mutable object escapes.
questions.hint: Ask what a client can do with the object the accessor returns.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: choose the response that keeps a mutator postcondition true
questions.stem: A lamp class stores a bulb count that must stay between one and nine. A client calls setBulbs(12). Which response keeps the setter's postcondition true?

options.text: Report the precondition violation and leave the stored count alone
Store 12 and let the accessor expose the illegal value
options.misconception: a mutator must always update state

options.text: Ignore 12 so the getter keeps reporting the last good value
options.misconception: silence makes a rejection complete

options.text: Clamp 12 down to 9 before storing the reduced count
options.misconception: silent coercion is standard validation

questions.explanation: The caller owns the precondition that the argument lies in range, so the class either reports the violation or leaves its own state untouched. Storing the raw value breaks the postcondition that the count is always legal, and clamping looks considerate but quietly substitutes a value the caller never asked for, so a bug upstream never surfaces.
questions.hint: Separate what the client promises from what the object promises.

questions.learningObjective: explain why reference equality fails for a String field
questions.stem: A Student class holds a private String name and defines equals as return name == other.name. Two students are each built from a separate new String("Mesa"). What does the call return?

options.text: false, because == compares references, not characters
true, because both fields hold the same characters
options.misconception: matching text makes == compare equal

options.text: true, because Java pools every String it builds
options.misconception: all String construction is pooled

options.text: false, because == cannot be applied to objects at all
options.misconception: == is illegal on object references

questions.explanation: Value semantics demand name.equals(other.name); == on two separately constructed Strings compares addresses, and only literals or explicitly interned text share an address. The trap is assuming the compiler folds two constructions into one pooled object, which it never does for new String calls, so identical text still compares as unequal.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two name fields point at the same String object.

questions.learningObjective: state the direction of the equals and hashCode contract
questions.stem: A catalog entry class overrides equals to compare title and edition, and overrides hashCode using only the shelf number. Which rule of the two-override contract is broken?

options.text: Equal entries can land in different hash buckets
Unequal entries can collide in the same hash bucket
options.misconception: collisions are forbidden by contract

options.text: hashCode may only read fields that equals ignores
options.misconception: the two overrides must use disjoint fields

options.text: hashCode must be recomputed from inside equals
options.misconception: equals should delegate to hashCode

questions.explanation: The contract imposes exactly one direction: equal objects must return equal hash codes. Reading fewer fields in hashCode than in equals breaks precisely that, so two copies of one title stored on different shelves hash apart and a lookup misses. Bucket collisions are legal and only slow a lookup, which is why option B feels like the violation but is not.
questions.hint: Decide which direction of implication the contract actually states.

questions.learningObjective: predict a failed hash lookup after a mutator changes a hash input
questions.stem: A frame object overrides hashCode as 31 * width + height and is used as a key in a HashMap. After setWidth(40) the program looks the frame up with the same reference. What happens?

options.text: The lookup fails, because the reference now hashes to a new bucket
The lookup succeeds, because the map stored the frame object itself
options.misconception: a map remembers its keys by identity

options.text: The lookup fails, because hashCode may only read final fields
options.misconception: the compiler bans mutable hash inputs

options.text: The lookup succeeds, because the map rehashes on every get call
options.misconception: lookups recompute the whole table

questions.stem: A seat class stores a row and a number, and its toString reads both fields. A client calls setRow(4) and then prints the object. What must a correct toString guarantee?

The text reflects only the values given to the constructor

options.misconception: toString results are cached for reuse

options.misconception: a stable string is the whole contract

questions.stem: Trace this range check: class G { private int points; G(int points) { if (points < 0 || points > 100) { throw new IllegalArgumentException("range"); } this.points = points; } int getPoints() { return points; } } int result = 0; try { result = new G(120).getPoints(); } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { result = -1; } System.out.print(result); What prints?

questions.explanation: Both overrides read the plot id, so all three records hash to one bucket where the partial equals calls them the same and a single entry remains. The tempting answer counts the stored species strings, but a set keeps one element per distinct key, and state that equals ignores cannot hold two records apart, so the override has to carry the whole identity the class claims.
questions.hint: Ask what two records must differ in to count as different.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: detect a mutator that edits the caller's own object
questions.stem: A mailbox adopts a caller's list and empties it: class M { private ArrayList<String> inbox; void adopt(ArrayList<String> incoming) { incoming.clear(); inbox = incoming; } } A client builds a list of three messages, calls adopt(list), and then prints list.size(). What does the client see?

options.text: zero, because the mutator cleared the list it was handed
three, because a mutator may not touch its own argument
options.misconception: arguments are private copies on call

options.text: one, because clear leaves the most recent element behind
options.misconception: clear removes all but one element

options.text: a thrown error, because clear on a shared list is forbidden
options.misconception: the runtime blocks aliasing writes

questions.explanation: Java passes references, so incoming names the client's own list, clear empties that very list, and the object then keeps the emptied list as its state. The tempting answer is three, built on the belief that parameters arrive as private copies, but a mutator that also edits its argument is a side effect on the caller that no accessor contract ever promised.
questions.hint: Ask what object the parameter name refers to.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: select the single change that removes a leak from a final field
questions.stem: A seat holder is written as public final class S { private final int[] seats; S(int n) { seats = new int[n]; } int[] slots() { return seats; } }. A client runs S s = new S(3); s.slots()[1] = 9;. Which single change makes the observed state trustworthy?

options.text: Return seats.clone() from the accessor
Drop the final keyword from the seats field
options.misconception: final is what lets a client write through

options.text: Store a single int count field instead of the array
options.misconception: a different field type stops aliasing

options.text: Add a setter that validates the requested index
options.misconception: a checked setter intercepts direct writes

questions.explanation: final only promises the reference never changes, so a client holding the returned array can still write through it, which is exactly what the traced call does; handing out a clone makes the internal array unreachable from outside, so state can change only through the class's own code. The tempting answer is D because a validated setter looks like a gate, but the client never passes through it when the accessor gives away the array itself.
questions.hint: Ask whether the client still shares the array object.

seats = initial;
options.misconception: reassigning the field shares the caller data

options.text: for (int i = 0; i < seats.length; i++) { }
options.misconception: an empty loop over the field copies it

options.text: initial[0] = 0;
options.misconception: clearing the source protects the field

questions.explanation: Allocating the field is only half the work: the values must be written into it, and arraycopy fills every slot from the caller's array while leaving the caller free to change its own data afterwards, so first still reports the original value. The tempting choices are the empty loop, which looks busy but copies nothing, and the field reassignment, which looks tidy yet hands the object's only array straight back to the caller.
questions.hint: Ask what still separates the field from the caller's array.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: judge which candidate sentences state true contract obligations
questions.stem: A designer is writing the contract for a new class and four candidate sentences are on the table. Which of them state a true obligation? Select all that apply.

options.text: A precondition is a condition the caller must establish before the call
A postcondition is what the object guarantees after the call returns
A postcondition is a check the caller makes before the call
options.misconception: postconditions are the caller's entry check

options.text: A precondition holds automatically once the object stores the value
options.misconception: storing a value proves it was legal

questions.explanation: A precondition is an entry condition the caller owes the object, and a postcondition is the exit guarantee the object owes its caller, which is why a class that cannot trust its input must check the precondition itself and must always establish the postcondition. The tempting answers C and D both put the obligation on the wrong side of the call: a postcondition describes what holds afterwards rather than before, and storing a value says nothing about whether it satisfied the requirement.
questions.hint: Ask which side of the call each kind of condition belongs to.
